diagnostic_evidence.quote:
Now let $\lambda$ be a singleton eigenvalue of
$\cDo(d)$ with a right eigenvector $x$.

Hence, $A$ is $\kappa$-optimally diagonally preconditioned
if, and only if, the orthonormal eigenvector pair satisfies
x_1\bullet x_1 = x_n\bullet x_n.

issues.failure_explanation: The derivative lemma requires simple eigenvalues, but the theorem extends its gradient and single-pair stationarity argument through multiplicities. This is false, not merely unproved. Take A=I₃+eeᵀ. Its largest eigenvector is e/√3, its minimum eigenspace is e⊥, and it is diagonally κ-optimal: permutation invariance and convexity of the sublevel sets make the averaged scaling proportional to e at least as good as any scaling. Yet no real unit vector in e⊥ has all three squared coordinates equal to 1/3, since three signs cannot sum to zero. Nonsmooth stationarity can require convex combinations of squared eigenvectors rather than one pair.

failure_location.quote:
In the nonsmooth case, we can choose the normalized
$x_1$, respectively, $x_n$, in the eigenspace of 
$\lambda_{\max}(\cDo (d))$, respectively $\lambda_{\min}( \cDo (d))$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the displayed gradient formula to differentiability points. Replace the nonsmooth single-pair condition by equality of convex combinations of squared unit eigenvectors from the two extremal eigenspaces, and prove the corresponding subdifferential stationarity criterion.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted necessary-and-sufficient characterization fails for repeated extremal eigenvalues. The later results explicitly restricted to simple extrema, and the independently proved quasisubgradient inclusions, are not invalidated.
issues.title: The nonsmooth optimality condition incorrectly requires a single eigenvector pair
issues.why_classification: A contained nonsmooth optimality argument supplies a comparable characterization without excluding repeated eigenvalues, but merely adding a normalization or correcting notation cannot repair the false necessity claim.

issues.failure_explanation: Neither normalized-update algorithm checks whether its direction is zero before dividing by its norm. For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], the initial extremal eigenvalues are simple and their unit eigenvectors have identical squared coordinates. Thus s₁=0 and g₁=0. Both algorithms enter their initially enabled loops and perform 0/0 before updating the stopping criterion. The iterate sequences needed by the convergence theorems therefore need not exist, even on an already optimal input with simple extrema.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Before each normalized update, test for a zero direction and return the current optimal scaling. For the infinite-sequence analyses, extend a run that reaches such a point by constant iterates.
issues.overall_effect: Algorithms GD and Subgrad V are undefined on legitimate optimal inputs, so their convergence statements cannot apply unconditionally to all stated inputs.
issues.title: The convergence theorems allow undefined zero-normalized updates
issues.why_classification: A local zero-direction branch and constant continuation preserve the optimization guarantees and rates without changing the method away from a certified optimum.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Second, since \Cref{GD} is a subgradient method, in general it is not a descent method.
$\kappa_{*}^{j}=\min_{k=1}^{j} \kappa(\cDo(d_k))$.

issues.failure_explanation: The supported liminf conclusion implies convergence of the running minimum, not monotone convergence of the actual objective sequence. Monotonicity is demonstrably false: with A=diag(2,1), δ=0.1, and t_k=1/k, the first direction is (2,-2), giving d₂=(1−1/√2,1+1/√2). Its condition number is approximately 2.914, larger than κ(d₁)=2. This counterexample has nonzero directions and simple extrema, so adding the missing zero-direction branch does not resolve it.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the final assertion by κ_*^j decreasing to κ_*, and revise claims of convergence of the actual objective sequence to the liminf/best-so-far guarantee proved in the source.
issues.overall_effect: The paper does not establish its claimed monotone, full-sequence objective convergence. Its liminf and best-so-far conclusions remain available.
issues.title: A liminf guarantee is incorrectly promoted to monotone last-iterate convergence
issues.why_classification: The source-supported repair changes a full-sequence, monotone convergence guarantee into a liminf or best-so-far guarantee. This is a substantive change of guarantee type, not a local correction preserving the stated conclusion.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
\min \{\textdef{$\kappa(v):=\kappa(\cVo(v))$} : 
    e+Vv\geq \hat \delta e,\, v\in \Rnm \},
where $\kappa(v):=\infty$ if $e+Vv< \hat \delta e$ and $\hat \delta\in (0,1)$ is a scalar.

issues.failure_explanation: Normalization fixes the sum of the scaling coordinates at n, so the additional fixed floor cannot subsequently be satisfied by rescaling an arbitrary optimal ray. For A=diag(M,1), the unique normalized optimal scaling is (2/(M+1),2M/(M+1)), with condition number 1. If the permitted floor exceeds 2/(M+1), that optimum is excluded; the restricted minimum is Mδ/(2−δ), which can be arbitrarily large. Thus the compact problem is not equivalent for an arbitrary δ in (0,1).

failure_location.quote:
From a computational
stability perspective, it is more efficient to minimize an equivalent 
smaller dimensional formulation that is not positively homogeneous.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Prescribe an A-dependent floor that retains the incumbent sublevel set. For example, with a_min=min A_ii and a_max=max A_ii, choose 0<δ<a_min/(κ(A)a_max). The source's trace bound and the Rayleigh bound λ_min≤A_ii d_i show that every normalized scaling with κ(d)≤κ(A) satisfies this floor. Describe uncalibrated fixed-floor experiments as restricted problems.
issues.overall_effect: Optimality and complexity results for the truncated simplex do not automatically establish optimality for the original positive diagonal-scaling problem.
issues.title: An arbitrary normalized coordinate floor destroys the claimed equivalence
issues.why_classification: A short, computable parameter condition obtained from the paper's existing eigenvalue bounds restores equivalence for every positive definite A without changing the algorithmic framework or the stated order in ε.

issues.failure_explanation: The remark asserts the inclusion for arbitrary v, although the fractional-program lemma requires a positive denominator and the displayed expression requires positive weighted eigenvector norms. With A=I₂, the specified V=(1,−1)ᵀ/√2, and v=√2, one gets w=(2,0). Then λ_min=0 and the minimum-eigenvector denominator is zero. The claimed vector is undefined. More generally, outside the prescribed feasible domain κ(v) is extended-valued, not the finite ratio used in the argument.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require v to belong to the stated feasible set, with the corresponding w≥δe, before asserting the quasisubgradient inclusion.
issues.overall_effect: The remark is false as an unrestricted assertion on R^(n−1); its intended feasible-point uses can remain valid.
issues.title: The nonhomogeneous quasisubgradient assertion omits its finite-domain hypothesis
issues.why_classification: Adding the standard domain hypothesis makes the cited positive-denominator argument applicable and preserves every intended algorithmic use.

It is immediate to see that $\hat \Omega$ is a convex compact set and that

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed simplex represents w≥δe only for the particular V=(1/√2)[I;−eᵀ], whereas Subgrad V permits any basis matrix. The positivity and Lipschitz arguments therefore do not cover its stated input contract. For n=2, A=diag(2,1), δ=1/2, and the allowed V=(2,−2)ᵀ, the initial direction is g₁=8. The first projected step is v₂=−1/√2, since the fixed simplex is [−1/√2,1/√2]. Consequently w₂=(1−√2,1+√2), and A Diag(w₂) is indefinite. The positive-denominator objective and quasisubgradient framework have already failed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the algorithm and theorem explicitly to the displayed special basis V. Alternatively, replace the fixed simplex by the actual pullback {v:e+Vv≥δe} for each supplied V and revise the projection implementation.
issues.overall_effect: The nonasymptotic theorem does not establish its guarantee for all basis matrices admitted by Subgrad V. The special-basis Lipschitz result cannot be applied to those other inputs.
issues.title: The complexity guarantee applies a special-basis simplex to arbitrary basis inputs
issues.why_classification: The least repair is a local restriction to the basis already used to derive the formulation. It preserves all matrix inputs, the intended inexpensive projection, and the ε-complexity order.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \frac{\kappa(A)-\kappa(EAE)}{\kappa(A)}*100
\Cref{alg:GDeplustVv} uses a maxiter of $80$ and also takes its main tolerance to be $10^{-4}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The tables establish objective reductions and PCG performance, not a common near-optimality guarantee. In the n=2200 row, the competing method increases κ by about 49%, while the reported alternative reduces it by about 71%. Thus the former output has value about 1.49κ(A), while the optimum is at most 0.29κ(A): its ratio to the optimum is at least approximately 5.1. This is a concrete large optimality gap, irrespective of stopping tolerances. The finite iteration limits and stopping tests also supply no general certificate that the other reported outputs are near-optimal.

failure_location.quote: In \Cref{PCG Linear Systems}, we find near $\kappa$-optimal diagonal preconditioners for a large collection of matrices using our subgradient method and the method in \cite{doi:10.1287/opre.2022.0592}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Describe these as candidate or computed diagonal preconditioners and report the observed reductions without claiming near-optimality. Reserve near-optimality claims for outputs accompanied by a valid optimal-value bound or gap certificate.
issues.overall_effect: The characterization of the reported finite-run outputs as near-optimal is unsupported and contradicted for some outputs. The measured reductions and PCG comparisons need not be discarded.
issues.title: The experiments call outputs near-optimal despite reported large optimality gaps
issues.why_classification: A limited weakening of the experimental optimality claim preserves the numerical comparisons, but a genuine near-optimality claim would require additional certification rather than an editorial clarification.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \State set $\Delta v_{k}\leftarrow -\nabla \kappa (v_k)$;
\Statex compute a min eigenpair $(\lambda_n^{1},x_n^{1})$ and max eigenpair $(\lambda_1^{1},x_1^{1})$ of $A$;

where $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_n$ have multiplicity one and
$x_1$ and $x_n$ are assumed to be normalized.

issues.failure_explanation: Even interpreting the formula as a valid subgradient at repeated extrema does not make its negative a descent direction. Use the specified V for n=3, u=(2,1,1)/√6, A=I+uuᵀ, z=(−1,1,1)/√3, and r=(0,1,−1)/√2. Both (z+r)/√2 and (z−r)/√2 are unit minimum eigenvectors. Their computed subgradients g₊ and g₋ satisfy g₊ᵀg₋=−13/24, so the directional derivative along −g₊ is at least 13/24>0. This point is not optimal: the feasible w-direction (−2,1,1) has directional derivative −2. Consequently no sufficiently short positive backtracking step gives nonincrease; quasiconvexity also rules out a later nonincreasing point on that ray. The required gradient can itself be undefined at multiplicities.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Introduce a genuine nonsmooth descent-direction selection, for example using the minimum-norm element of the full extremal-eigenspace subdifferential, with a zero-stationarity termination test. Use actual directional derivatives in the line-search conditions and specify finite failure handling.
issues.overall_effect: The line-search subroutine, and hence alg:GDeplustVv, can fail to return an admissible positive step at a nonoptimal positive definite input. Correcting the nonsmooth optimality theorem alone does not make an arbitrary subgradient a descent direction.
issues.title: Backtracking along an arbitrary negative eigenpair subgradient need not admit any step
issues.why_classification: Repair requires a contained but nontrivial change to the direction oracle and line-search logic. A scalar zero-direction check or smaller backtracking factor cannot fix the exhibited nonoptimal ascent direction.
